**Case Vignette: "David"**

David is a 26-year-old, soft-spoken man of South Eastern Asian descent who presents to therapy at the urging of his manager. He works as a bank teller in a busy downtown branch. During our first session, he sits with his shoulders hunched forward, his hands clasped tightly in his lap. He avoids eye contact, his gaze fixed on a spot on the carpet. He tells me he’s not sure why he’s here. “I’m just tired,” he says, his voice barely above a whisper. “Everyone says I’m not myself.”

The event that fractured his life happened eight months ago. He was on his lunch break, walking to a sandwich shop a block from his bank. He remembers the day was unseasonably warm. He remembers checking his phone for a text from his then-wife, a small, bitter habit he had developed. Then, the sound. Not a bang, he clarifies, but a percussive *thump* that he felt in his chest before he heard it. A pressure wave. Then, the screaming.

A homemade bomb had detonated inside a small café two doors down from where he stood. He was not physically injured. He was not the target. But the world for him, in that instant, became a different place. He froze, watching people run, their faces masks of primal terror. He saw a man on the ground, his leg bent at an unnatural angle. The air filled with the smell of burning sugar and something acrid, metallic. He stood there, a statue of shock, until a police officer physically grabbed his arm and pulled him away.

In the weeks that followed, David tried to return to normal. He went back to work. But the bank, once a place of routine and quiet order, became a cage of vulnerability. The line of customers felt like a threat. The large glass windows at the front of the building felt like an invitation. Every time the heavy vault door clicked shut, his heart would hammer against his ribs. He began to scan every person who entered, looking for bulges in jackets, for backpacks left unattended, for the tell-tale signs of someone who might not be there to deposit a paycheck. He started taking his lunch break at his desk, eating a granola bar while staring at his computer screen. The smell of coffee, once a comfort, now makes him nauseous.

His marriage, already strained, could not survive his silence. He couldn’t explain to his wife why he would wake up in a cold sweat, his hands gripping the sheets, the image of the man’s twisted leg seared onto the back of his eyelids. He couldn’t tell her that the sound of a car backfiring on their street would send him diving for cover behind the sofa. He grew irritable, snapping at her for small things, for turning the music up too loud, for surprising him from behind. He felt he was living behind a pane of glass, watching the world from a safe, but isolated, distance. She left three months ago. He doesn't blame her.

Now, David lives alone in a small apartment. He has stopped going to the gym, a place he once enjoyed. He finds loud noises unbearable. The hum of the fluorescent lights at the bank feels like a drill in his skull. He has a constant, low-grade headache. He is hypervigilant. On his walk to work, he has mapped out every potential hiding spot—an alleyway, a recessed doorway, a thick concrete pillar. He feels a constant, nagging sense of dread, as if the very atmosphere is charged with the potential for violence. He says he feels “broken,” but not in a dramatic way. It’s more like a quiet, persistent malfunction. He is a ghost in his own life, going through the motions of a man he no longer recognizes.
